note: Existing-source public educational gallery: CC photos and explicitly credited Bob Harms science/education-only photographs are distinguished. Source labels and arrows are not independent specimen voucher certification.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — BEARDED STEM NODE
tiles.details: First find a genuine CULM node, NOT the base of a leaf blade or a fluffy flowering rachis. New real cane photos 5 and 6 show thick rings of long ascending soft hairs at true stem joints on a research-grade Williamson County plant. Photo 5 has a millimeter ruler beside two photographed nodes. Then compare the broader silvery head to KR and silver. Published hair-length ranges remain source claims, not independent direct measurements from the ruler pixels.
tiles.short: Find the conspicuous pale hair beard on a TRUE culm joint, then trace the same stem to a many-branched silvery head.
tiles.status: ACTUAL TRUE BEARDED CULM NODES PHOTO-VERIFIED WITH RULER

tiles.heading: 02 · ROOTED PERENNIAL AND TRUE LIGULE
tiles.details: See panels 7–8 for an OUTER blade–sheath junction and a distinct hairy upper sheath margin; neither proves an exposed free inner membranous ligule. Panel 10 shows a living bunch above soil with roots hidden. The actual true CULM nodes with a physical millimeter ruler are on panel 5, not on the collars. A peeled-open 1–3 mm inner ligule and genuinely excavated connected fibrous roots are still missing.
tiles.short: Warm-season bunchgrass; culms usually 60–120 cm; TRUE membranous ligule approximately 1–2 mm.
tiles.status: PARTIAL PHOTO EVIDENCE — actual node/collar/aboveground bunch; free inner ligule and roots absent

tiles.heading: 03 · MANY RACEMES, TWO SPIKELETS PER PAIR
tiles.details: Texas A&M describes a dense often fanlike panicle; USFS gives individual racemes about 2–7 cm. On a mature branch identify the larger sessile fertile spikelet and the stalked smaller usually sterile or male companion. A source-identified paired-spikelet JPEG is recorded, but lacks calibrated local dissection. Do not arrow a whole raceme as a single spikelet.
tiles.short: Silvery panicle approximately 5–14 cm; numerous branches; sessile fertile and smaller pedicelled companion spikelets.
tiles.status: REAL SOURCE PHOTO — SCALED PAIR STILL MISSING

tiles.heading: 04 · GLUMES, LEMMA AND TWISTED AWN
tiles.details: Separate both glumes from a ripe sessile spikelet. The lower glume may have a dorsal pit OR no pit, so absence does not exclude cane. Within the glumes, the slender upper fertile LEMMA bears the long knee-bent, twisted AWN, not the glume. Record individual glume length and the real awn insertion with a 1-mm ruler before making microscopic arrows.
tiles.short: Sessile spikelet about 4.5–7.3 mm; two firm glumes, one lower sterile floret, one upper fertile floret; awn 20–35 mm.
tiles.status: PUBLISHED TRAIT — MEASURED LOCAL ANATOMY PENDING

tiles.heading: 05 · CANE VS INVASIVE KR AND SILVER BLUESTEM
tiles.details: PHOTO COMPARISON NOW PRESENT: panel 0 is actual CANE paired silky flowering head, panel 2 is introduced TEXAS KR bluestem (Tyler Cannon CC BY 4.0) with typically longer more fingerlike branches, and panel 3 is native SILVER bluestem (Matt Lavin CC BY-SA 2.0) with dense cottony shorter rames. Those panels are different source-matched species and their own archived local files; no borrowing as cane anatomy. The critically conspicuous bearded TRUE cane CULM node, actual short inner MEMBRANOUS ligule and fully measured sessile/pedicelled pair are STILL missing. Do not authorize removal using flowering architecture alone.
tiles.short: Cane: conspicuously bearded true nodes and many silvery fanlike branches; KR: more fingerlike branches and different paired spikelet proportions.
tiles.status: TWO LICENSED EXACT LOOK-ALIKE PHOTOS INSTALLED IN GALLERY — REAL NODE/INNER LIGULE PENDING

tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE AND HANDOFFS
tiles.details: Actual cane images now include six licensed, source-matched Texas anatomical/habit photographs from research-grade Williamson County observation 196400646, including physical ruler next to a true nodal beard. Existing specimen/source archived media remains preserved, and KR/silver photos are labeled as OTHER species. Total verified score is 3.5/6 (58.3%); full 70% goal needs opened inner ligule, exposed roots or convincing complete pair. The 3 Joey study photos remain image-specific CC BY-NC and are not assumed unrestricted. Rights-filtered GitHub Pages publication must pass independently.
tiles.short: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS: strong field clue, but decisive same-plant anatomy and rights-filtered site QA remain.
tiles.status: 58.3% PHOTO-ROLE COVERAGE — TRUE NODE FINISHED, INNER LIGULE/ROOTS HOLD

steps.title: 1 · Recognize the many-branched silvery head
steps.look_for: Silky long-awned flowering units cluster along multiple branching rames in John Rusk's source-confirmed cultivated cane bluestem.
steps.why_it_matters: Find the right family of grasses, but an individual fluffy head is not enough to authorize removal.

steps.title: 2 · Locate a living native Texas clump
steps.look_for: Inspect the attached aboveground culms and leaves in a natural rocky-soil stand from Brushy Creek, Williamson County. Roots are hidden.
steps.why_it_matters: An in-ground bunch is field context, not a photograph proving rhizome or fibrous root structure.

steps.title: 3 · FIND THE TRUE BEARDED NODE WITH MILLIMETER RULER
steps.look_for: Two real cane stem nodes have strong pale-white soft hair rings; the physical millimeter rule alongside is real. Follow each upright culm through the actual node.
steps.why_it_matters: This is cane bluestem's strongest distinguishing field trait versus invasive KR; do not mistake the separate flowering hair mass for a stem joint.

steps.title: 4 · Confirm the bearded node on a living stem
steps.look_for: Two separate actual flowering stalks have hairy white soft beard rings at TRUE nodes, not where leaves arise from a sheath.
steps.why_it_matters: This makes the key feature recognizable without a ruler and shows natural variation in the beard.

steps.title: 5 · See the OUTER leaf collar, not an opened ligule
steps.look_for: A leaf blade emerges from the green wrapping sheath. No free membranous inner ligule rim is separately exposed in this image.
steps.why_it_matters: The blade–sheath collar is not the same structure as a bearded culm node. Open the INNER sheath for a proper ligule photo.

steps.title: 6 · Identify an awned reproductive unit next to a ruler
steps.look_for: See pale silky hairs, an elongated flowering unit and awns with real ruler markings; distinguish fine white hairs from longer firm awns.
steps.why_it_matters: A true dissected attached fertile sessile/pedicelled pair and lemma awn insertion still require closer images.

steps.title: 7 · Rule out invasive King Ranch bluestem
steps.look_for: This is real Texas KR, not cane. See fewer relatively long terminal fingerlike racemes, compared with cane's denser fan and its long-bearded culm nodes.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm cane at two true nodes before vegetation removal. When unsure, retain native candidates until diagnostic anatomy is checked.

panels.label: Cane bluestem — many branching silky racemes
panels.caption: John Rusk's authenticated source records sessile and pedicellate spikelets on cultivated cane bluestem, each about 5 mm. Silky branch architecture is visible. Do not infer actual glume veins, awn origins or node hairs from this view; cultivated California source, not a Texas voucher.
panels.creator: John Rusk

panels.caption: A whole flowering specimen can orient field recognition, but do not infer Hays provenance or distinguish node hairs from a distant photograph.
panels.creator: Michel Chauvet
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: COMPARE — introduced KR bluestem, longer fingerlike flowering branches
panels.caption: THIS IS KING RANCH BLUESTEM, NOT CANE. On a genuine Texas CC BY 4.0 photograph, the narrow elongated racemes branch off near the top of the flowering culm. Compare cane's usually denser many-short-branched silver head at panel 0. These head architectures vary with maturity; do not certify a plant from branch count alone. Neither true ligule, fine glumes nor true bearded cane stem NODE is visible here.
panels.creator: Tyler Cannon
panels.modifications: CC BY photograph RGB JPEG re-encoded at <=2400px, EXIF/GPS removed; no pixel arrows added.
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: COMPARE — silver bluestem, cottony short rames in a narrower flowering head
panels.caption: THIS IS SILVER BLUESTEM, NOT CANE. Matt Lavin's source-identified CC BY-SA 2.0 close-up shows multiple short silky flowering rames forming a compact cottony head. Cane can have a fuller multi-branching fan and notably hairy TRUE culm nodes (off camera). Flowerheads may overlap: verify actual culm node and mature paired spikelets instead of calling silver/cane from color alone.

intro: Follow real cane-bluestem photographs from the whole flowering head to actual Texas bearded CULM nodes (one with a millimeter ruler), then compare an OUTER leaf collar and its hairy sheath edge, an awned flowering structure and invasive King Ranch. The free inner ligule and dug root crown remain unphotographed.
memory_rule: CANE = conspicuous LONG pale beard of soft hairs at true stem NODES plus a broad silvery branching fan; do NOT confuse node hairs with white flowering-head hairs or with upper leaf-sheath hairs.
safety_note: Photograph two true stem nodes and a mature head before removing a suspected invasive; if they cannot be seen, label Bothriochloa sp. Pending: actual peeled-open INNER 1–3 mm ligule with ruler, a dug root/rhizome crown, and a source-verified connected mature sessile/pedicelled spikelet pair. The licensed photographed cane belongs to an identified Williamson County specimen, not a documented Hays collection.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
comparison_text: Cane bluestem: true culm nodes bear a conspicuous beard of long soft hairs, with a relatively broad fan-shaped silvery inflorescence. Silver bluestem: contracted narrow woolly head with numerous shorter rames, usually pale smooth nodes. KR bluestem: generally several long thin radiating racemes in one terminal head; short node hairiness can vary so absence/presence of tiny hairs is not decisive. Little bluestem: separate short silky racemes repeatedly positioned along the upper leafy culm.
